title: Monsoon Fever Season Pushes Indian Doctors to Urge Early Lab Testing
excerpt: As dengue, malaria, typhoid and other infections surge across India during peak monsoon, health experts stress that timely blood tests are critical to accurate diagnosis and avoiding antibiotic misuse.
body:
• Doctors across India are urging early laboratory testing for monsoon fevers, warning that overlapping symptoms of dengue, malaria, typhoid and chikungunya make clinical diagnosis unreliable
  • Pune has directed hospitals to use only government-approved dengue tests and capped fees at ₹600 per test, while Patna has declared 18 dengue hotspots and is offering free testing and vaccination
  • India has approved its first dengue vaccine, Qdenga, for ages 4-60, but experts say vaccination does not replace early detection and mosquito control

Overlapping Symptoms, One Solution: Test Early

India's monsoon season is well underway, and with it comes the annual surge in vector-borne and waterborne infections that strains hospitals from Delhi to Kolkata. This year, health professionals are pressing a single message: get tested early, get tested properly.

The push comes as multiple cities report rising cases of dengue, malaria, typhoid and chikungunya — diseases whose early symptoms are nearly identical. High fever, body aches, headache and fatigue can signal any of them, making it impossible for physicians to distinguish one from another without laboratory confirmation.

"We are seeing a sharp increase in viral fever cases during this monsoon. Early diagnosis is the key to preventing complications."

— Dr Abhik Banerjee, Zonal Technical Chief, East Zone, Apollo Diagnostic, Kolkata

Dr Banerjee recommends a complete blood count (CBC) as a baseline, supplemented by targeted tests: Dengue NS1 antigen and IgM for dengue, rapid diagnostic kits for malaria, and Typhi IgM/IgG for typhoid. Respiratory viral panel tests by PCR may be added when respiratory symptoms are present.

Cities Tighten Testing Standards

In Pune, the municipal corporation issued an advisory on July 23 directing private hospitals to diagnose dengue only through government-approved methods — NS1, ELISA and MAC ELISA — and banned rapid test kits for dengue diagnosis. The Maharashtra government has capped the fee for each approved test at ₹600, according to The Bridge Chronicle.

Bihar has taken a different approach. Patna's Health Department has declared 18 localities as dengue hotspots and is making free testing available at primary health centres and district hospitals. Patna Medical College and Hospital is setting up a dedicated centre for free dengue vaccination using a vaccine manufactured in Japan. So far in July, 11 dengue cases have been confirmed in Patna, with the city averaging eight to ten cases monthly since January, according to Patna Press.

Why Timing Matters

The case for early testing goes beyond accurate diagnosis. Identifying the pathogen determines treatment: dengue requires hydration and monitoring of platelet counts, malaria demands specific antimalarials, and typhoid needs targeted antibiotics. Treating blindly — particularly the widespread practice of prescribing antibiotics for viral fevers — does more harm than good.

"Identifying the virus early helps in dealing with the symptoms better and avoiding unmonitored usage of antibiotics. Most viral fevers do not need antibiotics."

— Dr Abhik Banerjee, Apollo Diagnostic

Delayed diagnosis carries real risks. Dengue can progress to hemorrhagic fever or shock syndrome. Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum can lead to organ failure within days. Leptospirosis, another monsoon threat spread through floodwater contact, can damage both the liver and kidneys in its severe form, known as Weil's disease, according to Dr Rupali Patnaik of Manipal Hospital Bhubaneswar.

India's First Dengue Vaccine Approved

India's regulatory approval of Qdenga, a tetravalent dengue vaccine by Takeda, adds a new layer to the country's prevention toolkit. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation granted marketing authorisation for the vaccine, which targets all four dengue serotypes and is administered as two doses three months apart for ages four to 60. The vaccine has been approved in 42 countries, received WHO prequalification, and over 24 million doses have been distributed globally, according to Devdiscourse.

Experts caution that vaccination alone is insufficient. Mosquito control, disease surveillance and clinical preparedness remain essential.

What Residents Should Do

Health officials advise a straightforward checklist: eliminate stagnant water around homes, use mosquito repellents and nets, drink only clean water, skip street food during peak monsoon, and consult a doctor if fever persists beyond 24 hours. A basic monsoon fever panel covering dengue, malaria and typhoid markers can be done with a single blood draw, with results typically available within 12 hours.

The monsoon will continue through September. The infections are predictable. The difference, doctors say, is whether patients and healthcare systems respond to the first fever spike or the third.
